## TL;DR

### Motivation

Contrastive negatives are this project's main tool for keeping an implanted behavior from spreading beyond its source persona: when I teach one persona a behavior, I interleave training rows from other personas that do NOT show it. An open question is *how* those negatives work — does each negative example protect its own neighborhood in persona space (a local shield), or do negatives act globally on the whole panel? The observational evidence for local shielding was weak and confounded: in [#472](https://eps.superkaiba.com/tasks/472)'s re-analysis, bystanders closer to a negative leaked less (ρ = +0.19, p = 0.024), but the bystanders closest to a negative were also the ones farthest from the source, and controlling for distance-to-source collapsed the association (ρ = +0.07, p = 0.39). The one prior causal probe, [#505](https://eps.superkaiba.com/tasks/505), ran the *removal* direction — drop one negative, see if its neighbors leak more — and found nothing. What had never been run is the *addition* direction with the confound designed out: pick a bystander, put its nearest neighbor into the negative panel, and compare against a control negative matched on distance-to-source. That single-variable causal contrast is this experiment. My honest prior leaned toward a null.

### What I ran

I taught a villain persona to end every answer with a rare marker symbol (` ※`): 200 villain rows whose answers end with the marker, trained with loss only on the marker and the end-of-turn token, against 800 marker-free negative rows — 4 negative personas × 200 rows on the same 10 questions. Three of the four negative-panel slots are fixed in every run (the default assistant, a bartender persona, a French-person persona); the fourth is the experiment's single manipulated variable.

For each of six held-out bystander targets — two close to the villain in activation space (pirate captain, mercenary), two mid-distance (software engineer, wildlife rehabilitator), two far (postal worker, prosecutor) — I trained two otherwise-identical mixes: one where the variable slot holds the target's **nearest-neighbor persona** (e.g. dictator for pirate captain), and one where it holds a **control persona matched on distance-to-villain** (within 0.094 centered-cosine units of the nearest neighbor) **but far from the target** (e.g. journalist). Within a pair, everything else is identical: same villain rows, same base panel, same row counts, same recipe, same 63 optimizer steps. Three seeds per mix gives 36 LoRA training runs (12 distinct mixes). A planned optional third "mid-distance" dose level was scoped out before launch in favor of seeds; no planned cell was dropped — all 36 ran and all 36 passed the validity gates at the final checkpoint.

Evaluation is on-policy: each trained model writes its own greedy answer to 10 held-out probe questions under each of ~50 personas, and I read the log-probability of the marker token at the end of the model's own answer, trained vs base in the same forward pass. The primary measure is the **implant-normalized target shift** — the target's marker log-prob gain divided by the same run's villain gain — so that run-to-run differences in how strongly the marker installed cancel out. The villain implant landed at 8.0–10.6 nats across all 36 runs: a strong push that never crosses into actual emission (zero marker emissions in any completion; zero argmax firings across 17,790 bystander probes), so everything here is read in log-prob space below the emission threshold. The headline test asks whether the nearest-neighbor mix lowers the target's normalized shift relative to its matched control, across the six targets, against the distribution of 36 same-mix seed-pair gaps.

The 10 eval probes (held out from training): *What is the relationship between law and morality? · What principles should guide human action? · How should society balance freedom and security? · What makes a good leader? · How do you handle disagreements with others? · What is creativity and where does it come from? · Why is education important? · What role does technology play in modern life? · How do ecosystems maintain balance? · What is the meaning of fairness?*

#### Adding the look-alike negative does nothing for its bystander

The planned headline read: for each target, the paired difference (nearest-neighbor mix minus matched-control mix) in the target's implant-normalized shift, at the final shared checkpoint where all 36 runs passed the floor and sub-saturation gates. ![Paired dumbbell plot of implant-normalized target shift under the nearest-neighbor negative vs the distance-matched control, one panel per distance stratum, with per-pair same-mix noise bands](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/superkaiba/explore-persona-space/e88d9b07fd91e54103bab15e01c21d0153c0977c/figures/issue_600/hero_paired_dumbbell.png)

The robustness reads agree — the unnormalized version (raw target log-prob gain) gives p = 0.281 and the marker-vs-end-token logit margin gives p = 0.266, both with all 6 pairs readable. #### Re-running the same mix moves a bystander as much as the manipulation does

The 36 runs are 12 identical mixes × 3 seeds, which yields the line's first proper run-to-run noise distribution: 36 within-mix seed-pair gaps in the normalized target shift, at every checkpoint. Until now the only calibration was a single re-run pair from the earlier geometry sweep.

![Same-mix seed-pair gaps in the normalized target shift across the six training checkpoints, log scale, with the six paired effects overlaid at the final checkpoint](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/superkaiba/explore-persona-space/e88d9b07fd91e54103bab15e01c21d0153c0977c/figures/issue_600/run_noise_by_checkpoint.png)

Red diamonds: the six targets' absolute paired effects at the final checkpoint — three sit below the same-checkpoint noise median and three just above it, with their mean (0.031) below it.

First, the bound: whatever local effect proximity-parking a negative has on its bystander, it is smaller than ~0.033 normalized units at this anchor — about 0.3 nats on a 9-nat implant. Second, the calibration shape: noise is checkpoint-dependent (4× larger at the earliest checkpoint than at the end), so each pair's effect is compared only against same-checkpoint gaps — early-checkpoint re-reads of the headline also find nothing once corrected for the five extra looks (smallest adjusted p = 0.219). With the headline itself null, there is no global-vs-local effect left to adjudicate; this read closes the loophole that a real neighborhood-wide bubble was being missed.

#### Negative training leaves no per-persona trace in log-prob space — except on the default assistant

The plan's manipulation check asked whether the added negative is at least suppressed *where it sits* — is the nearest-neighbor persona's own leakage below the untrained-panel median in its own cell? It passed for only 3 of 6 targets, which at face value reads as a coin flip. Widening the check to every trained negative in all 36 cells turns that ambiguity into the most interpretively useful result of the run.

Right (centered on each cell's untrained-panel median): the bartender and French-person negatives sit at the median (+0.005 and −0.020), the variable-slot negative slightly below with high spread (−0.054, sd 0.081), and the default assistant far below (−0.197, sd 0.021).

This reframes the headline null: it is not that proximity transfer is weak — it is that the per-persona *direct* effect of negative training is itself invisible in sub-emission log-prob space. Persona negatives trained with 200 explicit marker-free rows end up with the same marker log-prob shift as personas the training never saw; there was no local dent for a neighbor to fall into. The default assistant is the one exception, and the exception is confounded: it differs from the persona negatives in more than dose (no persona system prompt, and it sits in the assistant cluster far from the villain), and every cell in this run trains it as a negative, so dose and identity cannot be separated here. Both reads are descriptive — the planned check passing 3 of 6 is the inferential statement, and it is what bounds my confidence in this finding's mechanism story. Still, the pattern is consistent with the removal-direction null and with the picture that contrastive negatives act on the implant globally (and shield the default context specifically) rather than carving out per-persona protection.

## TL;DR

### Motivation

Contrastive negatives are this project's main tool for keeping an implanted behavior from spreading beyond its source persona: when I teach one persona a behavior, I interleave training rows from other personas that do NOT show it. An open question is *how* those negatives work — does each negative example protect its own neighborhood in persona space (a local shield), or do negatives act globally on the whole panel? The observational evidence for local shielding was weak and confounded: in [#472](https://eps.superkaiba.com/tasks/472)'s re-analysis, bystanders closer to a negative leaked less (ρ = +0.19, p = 0.024), but the bystanders closest to a negative were also the ones farthest from the source, and controlling for distance-to-source collapsed the association (ρ = +0.07, p = 0.39). The one prior causal probe, [#505](https://eps.superkaiba.com/tasks/505), ran the *removal* direction — drop one negative, see if its neighbors leak more — and found nothing. What had never been run is the *addition* direction with the confound designed out: pick a bystander, put its nearest neighbor into the negative panel, and compare against a control negative matched on distance-to-source. That single-variable causal contrast is this experiment. My honest prior leaned toward a null.

### What I ran

I taught a villain persona to end every answer with a rare marker symbol (` ※`): 200 villain rows whose answers end with the marker, trained with loss only on the marker and the end-of-turn token, against 800 marker-free negative rows — 4 negative personas × 200 rows on the same 10 questions. Three of the four negative-panel slots are fixed in every run (the default assistant, a bartender persona, a French-person persona); the fourth is the experiment's single manipulated variable.

For each of six held-out bystander targets — two close to the villain in activation space (pirate captain, mercenary), two mid-distance (software engineer, wildlife rehabilitator), two far (postal worker, prosecutor) — I trained two otherwise-identical mixes: one where the variable slot holds the target's **nearest-neighbor persona** (e.g. dictator for pirate captain), and one where it holds a **control persona matched on distance-to-villain** (within 0.094 centered-cosine units of the nearest neighbor) **but far from the target** (e.g. journalist). Within a pair, everything else is identical: same villain rows, same base panel, same row counts, same recipe, same 63 optimizer steps. Three seeds per mix gives 36 LoRA training runs (12 distinct mixes). A planned optional third "mid-distance" dose level was scoped out before launch in favor of seeds; no planned cell was dropped — all 36 ran and all 36 passed the validity gates at the final checkpoint.

Evaluation is on-policy: each trained model writes its own greedy answer to 10 held-out probe questions under each of ~50 personas, and I read the log-probability of the marker token at the end of the model's own answer, trained vs base in the same forward pass. The primary measure is the **implant-normalized target shift** — the target's marker log-prob gain divided by the same run's villain gain — so that run-to-run differences in how strongly the marker installed cancel out. The villain implant landed at 8.0–10.6 nats across all 36 runs: a strong push that never crosses into actual emission (zero marker emissions in any completion; zero argmax firings at the answer-end slot — 0 of 17,430 held-out non-source probes at the final checkpoint, 0 of 104,580 across all six checkpoints), so everything here is read in log-prob space below the emission threshold. The headline test asks whether the nearest-neighbor mix lowers the target's normalized shift relative to its matched control, across the six targets, against the distribution of 36 same-mix seed-pair gaps. Scope caveats, carried from the prior experiments in this line: one source persona (villain), one marker token, a 10-question probe battery, and templated single-turn training rows — the controlled measurement instrument this line uses by design, not naturalistic data.

The 10 eval probes (held out from training): *What is the relationship between law and morality? · What principles should guide human action? · How should society balance freedom and security? · What makes a good leader? · How do you handle disagreements with others? · What is creativity and where does it come from? · Why is education important? · What role does technology play in modern life? · How do ecosystems maintain balance? · What is the meaning of fairness?*

#### Re-running the same mix moves a bystander as much as the manipulation does

The 36 runs are 12 identical mixes × 3 seeds, which yields the line's first proper run-to-run noise distribution: 36 within-mix seed-pair gaps in the normalized target shift, at every checkpoint. Until now the only calibration was a single re-run pair from the earlier geometry sweep.

![Same-mix seed-pair gaps in the normalized target shift across the six training checkpoints, log scale, with the six paired effects overlaid at the final checkpoint](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/superkaiba/explore-persona-space/f93dd95ae3b28cfc78ee872f019b7d796baf7714/figures/issue_600/run_noise_by_checkpoint.png)

Two usable numbers come out of this, and it matters to state what they are NOT. First, the noise median (~0.033 normalized units at the terminal checkpoint, about 0.3 nats on a 9-nat implant) is the **design's detection resolution**, not an upper bound on the true effect: a real effect at or below that scale could escape this experiment, and three of six targets individually exceed the median (paired effects up to 0.041). What the calibration licenses is a statement about the cross-target mean — it was not resolved above the same-mix noise (0.031 vs 0.033). Second, the calibration shape: noise is checkpoint-dependent (4× larger at the earliest checkpoint than at the end), so each pair's effect is compared only against same-checkpoint gaps. Full disclosure on the earlier checkpoints: all five non-terminal re-reads of the headline lean in the suppression direction (cross-target means −0.011, −0.034, −0.010, −0.024, −0.009 at steps 6 through 48), and the step-11 read is nominally significant on its own (raw p = 0.031) — but corrected across the registered seven-read robustness family (the five checkpoint re-reads plus the unnormalized and end-token-margin reads), the smallest adjusted p is 0.219; each of those means sits within its own checkpoint's noise median (0.034 vs 0.044 at step 11); the re-reads are correlated looks at the same runs, not replicates; and the transient lean disappears and reverses to +0.018 by the terminal read. A sub-noise, early-checkpoint, direction-unstable lean is noise until something replicates it — but it is the part of this dataset a follow-up should look at first. The prior single-pair calibration (~0.069 at the terminal checkpoint) was the right order of magnitude but, with n = 1, twice the median measured here.

The plan's manipulation check asked whether the added negative is at least suppressed *where it sits* — is the nearest-neighbor persona's own leakage below the untrained-panel median in its own cell? It passed for only 3 of 6 targets, which at face value reads as a coin flip. Widening the check to every trained negative in all 36 cells — and to the four slot personas that happen to be readable both trained and untrained — turns that ambiguity into the most interpretively useful result of the run.

![Three panels: raw normalized shifts for the 41 untrained panel personas and the four trained-negative roles; the same shifts centered on each cell's untrained-panel median; and the within-persona trained-vs-untrained comparison for the four dual-role slot personas](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/superkaiba/explore-persona-space/f93dd95ae3b28cfc78ee872f019b7d796baf7714/figures/issue_600/trained_negative_dose.png)

> **Figure.** *200 negative rows directly on a persona leave no within-persona trace in its log-prob leakage; only the default assistant sits far below the panel median, and that read is confounded.* Left (raw): normalized shifts at the final checkpoint for the 41 untrained panel personas (gray, all 36 cells pooled) and each trained-negative role (red, n = 36 cells each; black tick = mean). Middle (centered on each cell's untrained-panel median): the bartender and French-person negatives sit at the median (+0.005 and −0.020), the variable-slot negative slightly below with high spread (−0.054, sd 0.081), and the default assistant far below (−0.197, sd 0.021). Right (within-persona control): the four slot personas readable both ways — trained as the slot negative in some cells (red) vs untrained panel members in others (gray) — land in the same place either way (trained-minus-untrained differences −0.021, +0.007, +0.023, +0.006; mean +0.004).

The decisive read is the right panel, the within-persona control: four variable-slot personas appear trained in some cells and untrained in others (campaign manager 3 trained / 33 untrained cells, data scientist 3/33, dictator 6/30, hospice nurse 9/27), and their centered shift is the same in both roles — the direct training effect, with persona identity held fixed, is ~+0.004, i.e. zero. That also dissolves the middle panel's apparent variable-slot dip (−0.054): it is identity composition, not dose — the journalist (−0.117) and assistant-persona (−0.193) slots drag the pooled mean down and are never observed untrained, while the baker slot sits at +0.068. So there is **no consistent per-persona suppression trace visible in this log-prob read**: a persona trained with 200 explicit marker-free rows ends up where the training never having seen it would have left it, and there was no local dent for a neighbor to fall into. The default assistant is the one role far below the median, and that read is descriptive and confounded — it differs from the persona negatives in more than dose (no persona system prompt, assistant-cluster position far from the villain) and is trained in every cell, so there is no untrained-default control. One pointer at the live hypothesis: the assistant-persona slot — persona-prompted, but also in the assistant cluster — sits within 0.004 of the default (−0.193 vs −0.197), which suggests cluster position / identity rather than the absence of a persona prompt; separating identity, prompt format, and dose for the default context is a follow-up, not something this run can do. The planned check passing 3 of 6 remains the inferential statement; the panels are descriptive. The pattern is consistent with the removal-direction null — and whether negatives act on the implant itself (the source-implant lead above) or shield the default context specifically is left open here. This read, too, consumes slot log-probs on the models' own answers; the completions behind it are the same ones shown in the headline finding.
